lessons.title: The well-formed dot point, taught explicitly

clauses.text: The dot point has three parts and always the same three: the feature, what it sounds like and where in the excerpt, then why it is there.
Terminology and structure are taught together, because a precise word in the wrong structure still loses the mark.
Three dot points on one short excerpt, marked live in front of you against the AT3 criteria.

criteria: I can write a dot point with a feature, a location and a reason.
I can tell a well-formed dot point from a vague one.

explain.title: The dot point, now against a marker's criteria

body.p: You already know the shape: a feature, what it sounds like and where, and why it is there. What's different in an examination response is that a real marker is checking each part against a criteria sheet, not just reading for sense.

body.h: What a marker is actually checking

ul: **The feature has to be named precisely.** “The rhythm” is not a feature. “Syncopation in the melody” is.
**The location has to be specific enough to check.** “Later in the piece” cannot be verified against the recording. A bar number, a timing, or a clearly identified section can.
**The reason has to connect to the feature you named**, not restate the general mood of the piece. If your reason would work unchanged for a different feature, it isn't doing its job.

body.p: A precise word in the wrong structure still loses the mark, and a correct structure with vague words loses it just as fast. Both have to be right at once, which is why this lesson marks live: seeing exactly where a real response gains or loses a mark is faster than being told the rule in the abstract.

lessons.title: One element per dot point: pitch and melody
lessons.contentPoint: Analysing elements in repertoire
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse pitch and melody precisely.
criteria: I can describe a melody's shape and range and say what it achieves.
steps: Pitch and melody in Australian repertoire: range, contour, intervals and where the melody sits in the texture.
The same excerpt heard three times with a different pitch question each time.
Timed writing: two dot points on melody, marked against the criteria.
lessons.enduring: Precision about one element beats vagueness about four.

body.lead: We are learning to analyse pitch and melody precisely.

clauses.text: Pitch and melody in Australian repertoire: range, contour, the intervals that give a tune its shape, and where the melody sits in the texture.
The same excerpt three times with a different pitch question each time. Repeated listening only works if the target changes.
Two dot points on melody, written to time. Precision about one element beats vagueness about four.

criteria: I can describe a melody's shape and range.
I can say what the melodic writing achieves.

body.p: Pitch and melody are two different questions asked together. Pitch is where the notes sit; melody is what they do once you put them in order.

ul: **Range** is the distance from the lowest note to the highest, described as wide or narrow rather than guessed at.
**Contour** is the overall shape as the melody moves: rising, falling, arch-shaped, or built from small repeated cells.
**Interval shape** is what actually gets you from one note to the next: stepwise movement sounds smooth, leaps sound more dramatic, and a melody that mixes both has decided where to spend each.
**Where the melody sits in the texture** matters as much as what it does: the same tune sung alone reads differently from the same tune buried under three other layers.

body.p: Precision beats coverage here. One dot point that nails the contour and says exactly what effect it creates is worth more than a dot point that mentions range, contour and interval all at once without landing on any of them. The lesson gives you the same excerpt three times because a different target each time forces exactly that kind of precision.

lessons.title: One element per dot point: texture and tone colour
lessons.contentPoint: Analysing elements in repertoire
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse texture and tone colour precisely.
criteria: I can describe the layers in an excerpt and what each contributes.
steps: Texture and tone colour analysed in three Australian works: how many layers, what each is doing, and what each sound source contributes.
Layer-by-layer listening with the mix isolated where recordings allow.
Timed writing: two dot points, marked against the criteria.
lessons.enduring: Texture is countable, and counting it is where the analysis starts.

body.lead: We are learning to analyse texture and tone colour precisely.

clauses.text: Texture and tone colour in three Australian works: how many layers there are, what each one is doing, and what each sound source contributes.
Layer by layer, with the mix isolated wherever the recording allows it. Texture is countable, and counting it is where the analysis starts.
Two dot points, written to time and marked against the criteria. One element each, as always.

criteria: I can describe the layers in an excerpt.
I can say what each sound source contributes.

body.p: Texture analysis starts with a number: how many layers are actually in the excerpt right now. Not felt, counted.

ul: **Count the layers.** Melody, harmony, bass, percussion — isolate each one in turn if the recording allows it, and say how many are sounding at once.

**Say what each layer is doing.** A layer can carry the melody, fill harmony underneath, mark the pulse, or add colour without doing any of those three. Two layers doing the same job is a different texture from two layers each doing something different.

**Tone colour is the source, not the pitch.** A guitar and a piano can play the same note and sound completely different — that difference is tone colour, and it needs its own vocabulary rather than being folded into “instrumentation”.

body.p: A texture answer that says “it builds up” has counted nothing. A texture answer that says “a solo voice at the opening becomes four layers by the second verse: melody, backing vocal, guitar and bass” has, and that second version is the one that scores.

lessons.title: Structure and duration in the same excerpt
lessons.contentPoint: Analysing elements in repertoire
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse structure and duration as separate questions.
criteria: I can map an excerpt's structure and describe its use of duration.
steps: Structure and duration: sections, proportions, metre, tempo and how the piece uses time.
One excerpt mapped for structure, then the same excerpt analysed for duration, so students feel the difference between the two questions.
Timed writing under examination conditions.
lessons.enduring: Two questions about time are not the same question.

body.lead: We are learning to analyse structure and duration as separate questions.

clauses.text: One excerpt mapped for structure: the sections, the order they come in, and how much time each one gets.
Then the same excerpt for duration: metre, tempo and how the piece uses time. Two questions about time are not the same question.
Timed writing under examination conditions, one dot point on each of the two.

criteria: I can map an excerpt's structure.
I can describe its use of duration without repeating the structure answer.

explain.title: Structure and duration are two separate questions

body.p: Both are about time, which is exactly why they get confused. Structure asks what order the sections come in and how big each one is. Duration asks how the piece moves through time from moment to moment: its metre, its tempo, its use of longer and shorter note values.

ul: **Structure** is the big shape: intro, verse, chorus, bridge, however many sections there are and in what order. Answering it means naming sections and their proportions, not just listing them.
**Metre** is how the beats are grouped, in twos, threes, fours, and whether it stays constant or changes.
**Tempo** is the speed of the pulse, and whether it is steady or moves.
**Use of duration** is the pattern of long and short note values across the piece, and what that pattern does to the feel.

body.p: The trap is answering a duration question with a structure answer, because both can sound like they're describing “what happens over time”. Ask which question was actually asked: does it want the shape of the piece, or the piece's relationship to the clock underneath it? They are graded separately, and a structure answer to a duration question earns nothing.

lessons.title: Protocols first
lessons.contentPoint: Place, Country and Languages, and protocols
lessons.intention: We are learning the protocols that govern how we study this music.
criteria: I can state the protocols that apply and why they exist.
steps: Before any listening: the protocols for studying the music of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.
What the class may do with this material, what it may not do, and why permission and attribution are not formalities.
The school's consultation process explained, including that repertoire for this block is chosen through it.
lessons.enduring: Protocols come before the listening, not alongside it.

body.lead: We are learning the protocols that govern how we study this music.

clauses.text: Before any listening: the protocols for studying the music of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples. They come first, not alongside.
What this class may do with the material, what it may not, and why permission and attribution are not formalities.
The works for this block are chosen through the school's consultation. They are named in class once that is done, and not before.

criteria: I can state the protocols that apply here.
I can say why they exist.

body.p: Before this block plays a single excerpt, the protocols that govern how this class studies music of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples are stated in full, because they apply to how the material is used, not just to what is said about it afterwards.

ul: **Permission is not a formality.** Music connected to Country, ceremony or community can carry restrictions on who may hear it, perform it, or discuss it, and those restrictions are set by the community it belongs to, not by this classroom.

**Attribution names the community, not just an artist.** Where a work comes from, and whose knowledge and Country it carries, is part of what has to be said about it correctly, every time it is discussed.

**Consultation decides what this class studies.** The specific works for this block are selected through the school's own consultation process, and named in class only once that process is complete, not before, and not by guesswork in the meantime.

body.p: These protocols are not a preamble to the listening that comes after. They are the condition the listening happens under. Everything this block does with a work, in class or in writing, applies them, and that starts here, before anything has been heard.

criteria: I can describe how a work reflects Place, Country or Languages.

explain.title: A work and the Country it belongs to

body.p: Describing how Place, Country and Languages appear in a piece of music is not the same task as describing its key or its instrumentation. It asks how the music itself carries a relationship to a specific Country, and that relationship is described in the terms the community itself uses for it, not in borrowed general language.

ul: **Language in the music is not decoration.** Where a song is sung in a Language, that Language carries meaning and connection that a translation does not fully hold, and analysis needs to say so rather than treat the words as incidental to the music.

**Place and Country can be reflected in sound as well as in words** — in the instruments used, in melodic material connected to a specific Country, or in how a work marks a relationship to land that a listener from outside it would not recognise unprompted.

**Use the community's own terms.** Where a source describes a relationship in specific language — a place name, a Language name, a description of significance — that is the correct term to use, not a generic substitute that sounds equivalent but isn't.

body.p: This is analysis under the same protocols as the previous lesson, applied now to how you write rather than only to how you listen. Getting the terms right is part of getting the analysis right, not a separate courtesy on top of it.

lessons.title: How music influences and challenges ideas
lessons.contentPoint: Music influencing and challenging ideas
lessons.intention: We are learning how music can influence and challenge ideas.
criteria: I can explain what a work argued and how the music carried the argument.
steps: Music as an argument: how a work can influence and challenge ideas at local, national and international levels.
One Australian work examined for what changed because of it.
Written response: two dot points, one on a musical feature and one on its effect.
lessons.enduring: Music does work in the world, and the working is audible.

body.lead: We are learning how music can influence and challenge ideas.

clauses.text: One Australian work examined for what changed because of it. Music does work in the world, and the working is audible.
The argument and the music that carries it are separated. A song can be right about something and still be badly made.
Two dot points: one on a musical feature, one on the effect that feature has.

criteria: I can explain what a work argued.
I can say how the music carried the argument.

guide.brief: One work, three moments in its arrangement. Press the name to play it from the top, or a time to drop into that moment.

cues.text: The band swells here, then pulls back within a few bars. Listen for the arrangement holding itself in rather than letting the moment grow.
The fullest and most sustained the arrangement ever gets, and the only point in the song where it stays this way for this long.
It fades rather than finishing on a chord. A work like this does not get a triumphant last note.

explain.title: Separating the argument from the music that carries it

body.p: A song can be right about something and still be badly made, and a song can be brilliantly made in service of an argument you disagree with. Judging the two together blurs both judgements, so this lesson asks for them apart.

ul: **What did the work argue?** State the argument itself, in your own words, the way you'd summarise any position, not the song's mood, its subject matter, or how it made you feel.

**What musical feature carried it?** Name a specific feature — a lyric delivered over a bare texture, a melody that stays plain rather than building, a specific instrumental choice — and say what that feature does to how the argument lands.

**Connect the two, in that order.** The feature only matters because of the effect it has on the argument's force. Naming a feature without saying what it does to the argument is description; saying what the argument was without naming how the music carries it is a lyric summary, not music analysis.

body.p: Music doing work in the world is not a metaphor: a listener's response to an argument really can change because of how it was set to music rather than only what was said. That working is what this pair of dot points is asking you to make audible.

patched.text: Unseen excerpt, checked against the register

explain.title: A method for something you've never heard

body.p: An unfamiliar excerpt is not a blank page. It's a task with an order, and the order matters more than how much you already know about the style.

ul: **First playing: get oriented.** Tempo, mood, obvious instrumentation, the genre if it's recognisable. Write almost nothing down; just build a mental frame to hang detail on.
**Second playing: hunt for detail.** Go section by section if you can, and write down specific, nameable features as you hear them, not afterwards from memory.
**Third playing: check and fill gaps.** Confirm what you wrote against what you actually hear this time, and fill in whatever you know is still missing rather than starting again from scratch.

body.p: Writing down everything on the first playing is the most common way to waste it: you end up chasing your own pen instead of listening, and you lose the overview that only comes from listening with nothing to write yet. Three playings, three different jobs, done in order, produces a fuller response than three identical attempts at the same job.

body.lead: We are learning to write about context in the form an examination expects.

clauses.text: Context in examination form: what the excerpt suggests about style, culture, history or society, in correct terminology and without invention.
A defensible inference and a guess look much the same on the page. Marked examples show what actually separates them.
Timed writing on context only. A context claim has to be supported by the sound, not by a hunch.

criteria: I can write a context statement supported by what I heard.

explain.title: A defensible inference, not a guess

body.p: A context sentence and a guess can look identical on the page. The difference isn't confidence, it's whether the claim is actually supported by something in the sound.

ul: **Start from a specific feature**, not a general impression. “This sounds old” is a guess; “the recording quality and the acoustic instrumentation suggest an early recording” is a claim built on something you can point to.
**Name the kind of context**, so the marker knows what you're claiming: style, culture, history or era, or the social or geographic setting the music suggests.

**Stop where the evidence stops.** A context sentence that goes further than what you actually heard, naming a specific date, a specific artist, a specific place, without evidence for that specificity, turns a defensible inference back into a guess, just a more detailed-sounding one.

body.p: The test is simple: could you point to the exact sound that led you to the claim? If yes, it's an inference. If the honest answer is “it just sounds like it”, it's a guess wearing an inference's sentence structure, and a marker can tell the difference even when you can't.

lessons.contentPoint: Context written up with correct terminology

body.lead: We are learning the technique that makes the paper survivable.

The full practice paper begun under timing. Technique is worth marks that knowledge alone does not collect.

criteria: I can budget my time across the paper.
I can use each playing for a different purpose.

body.p: The paper gives you the same excerpt three times, and using all three playings for the same task is the single biggest way marks get left behind, because it means two of the three genuinely earned nothing.

ul: **Read the question before the first playing.** You cannot listen efficiently for something you don't yet know you're being asked.
**Budget the time before you start writing**, against how many marks the question is worth, not against how much you feel like you have to say.
**Give each playing a different job**, orient, then detail, then check, the same order as an unfamiliar excerpt, because in the exam every excerpt is functionally unfamiliar.

body.p: The first playing produces nothing useful sometimes. That happens to everybody, and the recovery is the same either way: use the second playing to do what the first should have done, rather than panicking and hoping the third saves you. Technique like this is worth real marks on its own, separate from what you actually know about the music, which is exactly why it gets practised under real timing rather than talked about in the abstract.

explain.title: Studied against adapted: knowing which one you're allowed to do

body.p: Some music may be studied and discussed but not adapted or performed differently from how it was created, and knowing which situation you're in is the actual skill here, not a rule to recite, a judgement to make correctly every time.

ul: **Permission covers use, not just access.** Being able to hear a work, or even having studied it under the protocols already covered, does not automatically mean you have permission to arrange it. Those are two separate permissions.

**Attribution in an arrangement has to survive the changes you make.** Crediting the original creator and the tradition or community a work comes from doesn't stop being required just because you've changed the instrumentation or the style.

**Intellectual property here is not the same as ordinary copyright.** Some material carries community ownership and cultural protocols that continue to apply regardless of who holds a copyright, and a plan that only checks copyright has checked the wrong thing.

body.p: This is why the check happens before the work goes into the arrangement, not after: a plan is easy to redirect, and a finished arrangement of something that should not have been adapted is not.
